intro: You are the voice of one page on a small set of websites about the rules of physics. There are nine pages, one for each level, from the quark up to the whole universe. The first levels are a zoom out by size (quark, nucleus, the quantum rules, atom, molecules, crowds of particles); the last ones are different conditions (things our own size, light and high speed, heavy things and the cosmos). Every page has two sides. The front shows the rule in charge at that level. The visitor can flip the page over, and the back shows its reverse: what undoes, limits or follows from that rule. Each side is a short film with a narrator, drawn from measured numbers or worked out in the page from the real rule; the pictures say where each number comes from.
notes: Keep two kinds of claim apart. What experiments show (the stripes on the screen, the colors hydrogen gives off, clocks that run slow) is settled, and has been checked many times. What it means underneath is sometimes still open: what a quantum measurement really is, a mathematical proof that quarks can never get out, why the universe's expansion is speeding up and why two ways of measuring its rate disagree. Say which kind of thing you are talking about. The pictures are drawings: real atoms and nuclei are not little balls, bent space and time cannot be drawn flat, and several pictures exaggerate so an effect can be seen; say so if the visitor takes a picture too literally. You are an A.I., not a physicist who did these experiments: what you know comes from what people have published.

front.name: The Quark
front.sub: the smallest pieces we know · three of them make a proton · the rule down here: you can never pull one out
front.text: We are going to start as small as anyone has ever looked. This is a proton. It sits in the middle of every atom. And inside it are three even smaller things, called quarks. Here is the rule down here. A quark is never, ever, found alone. Something holds them together. Think of a stretchy string. Now watch what happens when you pull one quark away. The string doesn't get weaker. It keeps pulling just as hard, as hard as the weight of sixteen tonnes. So the further you pull, the more energy you pour in. And then, snap. The string breaks. But you don't get a loose quark. All that energy turns into two brand new quarks, one for each broken end. Nobody has ever caught a quark by itself. And here is the strange part. The three quarks are only about one hundredth of the proton's weight. Nearly all the rest is the energy of the pulling.
front.scene: THE QUARK. A proton (measured radius 0.84 femtometres, CODATA 2022) drawn with its three quarks joined by strings of the strong force. One quark is pulled away. A gauge beside it shows the real behaviour worked out by computer (lattice QCD): the pull stays about the same however far it is stretched, roughly 1 GeV for every femtometre, which is a force of about 160,000 newtons, the weight of 16 tonnes; so the energy stored grows steadily with distance. At about 1.25 femtometres the string snaps and its energy becomes a new quark and antiquark, one at each broken end: the proton is whole again and the quark that was pulled leaves as part of a pair. No quark has ever been seen alone. A last bar shows the proton's weight (938 MeV): its three quarks account for about 9 MeV, one hundredth (Particle Data Group quark masses); the rest is the energy of the strong force.

back.name: almost free
back.sub: asymptotic freedom · hit a quark hard and fast and it acts almost as if nothing held it · Nobel Prize 2004
back.text: On the front, quarks could never get away. Here is the opposite. Fire something tiny and very fast into a proton. For that one short moment, the quark it hits behaves almost as if it were free. As if there were no string at all. Scientists measure how strong the grip is, and the harder they hit, the weaker it gets. At gentle hits, the number is about a third. At the hardest hits, about a tenth. That is backwards from everything else we know. Magnets and gravity get weaker far away. This grip gets weaker up close. But the quark still doesn't escape. As it flies off, the string wakes up, snaps, and makes a spray of new particles. Three people worked out why, and won a Nobel Prize. Nobody has proved yet, with maths alone, that a quark can never get out.
back.scene: THE REVERSE OF "NEVER ALONE": almost free (asymptotic freedom). A fast electron is fired into a proton and knocks one quark; for that instant the quark moves as if nothing held it. A chart shows the measured strength of the strong force's grip (the coupling, alpha-s) against how hard the collision is: 0.31 at 1.78 GeV and 0.118 at 91 GeV (Particle Data Group, 2024), with a curve from the standard formula through the second point. It falls as the hit gets harder, the reverse of electricity, magnetism and gravity, whose grip is weaker far away. The struck quark still does not get out: as it flies off the string forms again, snaps, and makes a spray of new particles (a jet). Gross, Politzer and Wilczek explained this in 1973 (Nobel Prize 2004). That quarks can never get out has not been proved mathematically; it is one of the Clay Institute's unsolved million-dollar problems.
